content: One of the significant challenges in managing cardiovascular disease (CVD) in people living with HIV is the lack of high-quality data evaluating proven CVD therapies in this population. For instance, prospective trials investigating the use of statins in individuals with HIV have generally been small in scale and have not assessed critical clinical outcomes. Integrated disease campaigns conducted in Lesotho and Uganda, as part of the SEARCH consortium, which included CVD screening and HIV testing, have demonstrated the feasibility of combining communicable and non-communicable disease screenings within community-based HIV programs. Improved diagnosis and care linkage for CVD conditions have also been shown to enhance linkage to HIV care and antiretroviral therapy (ART). Since 2012, pilot programs integrating CVD and HIV services in Kenya, Nigeria, and Zambia have proven to be both feasible and acceptable, with CVD care incorporated into chronic HIV care models. Further research is needed to better understand the complex mechanisms of atherogenesis in people with HIV, clarify the relationships between traditional and HIV-specific CVD risk factors, and explore how ART influences these interactions. Studies on the impact of early ART initiation on CVD development, particularly in adolescents and children with HIV, are also necessary. Clinical research should focus on developing and validating risk prediction methods and strategies for reducing CVD risk in people with HIV. Simplified CVD screening protocols and risk assessment tools that account for HIV-specific factors need to be validated to improve accuracy. Additionally, the use of co-therapies for CVD, such as statins, aspirin, antihypertensive drugs, and metformin, and their effects on HIV-related mortality, should be evaluated. Research should also address the unique pathophysiology, associated risk factors, and optimal management of downstream CVD complications in HIV, such as heart failure and malignant arrhythmias, across both high-income and resource-limited settings. People living with HIV are at a heightened risk of mental, neurological, and substance-use disorders, with depression being one of the most prevalent mental health comorbidities. Systematic reviews from both lowand high-income countries have reported depression prevalence rates as high as 80% among people with HIV, though these rates vary widely due to differences in screening and diagnostic criteria. Depressive symptoms are particularly common in sub-Saharan Africa, where the HIV burden is also high. Depression in people with HIV is associated with poorer adherence to treatment. Despite the opportunity to detect and manage depression in chronic HIV care settings, it is often overlooked by healthcare providers. Untreated mental health disorders can negatively impact overall health, ART adherence, and retention in care, while also increasing the risk of side effects and drug interactions being missed. The WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) provides evidence-based guidelines for diagnosing and managing mental, neurological, and substance-use disorders, including depression. Implementing mhGAP through primary care has been shown to improve the detection and management of depression compared to standard care approaches. However, there is limited evidence on the impact of routine depression screening and management on ART adherence and treatment outcomes in people with HIV. While managing depression improves mental health and general well-being, there is insufficient evidence to confirm that it directly enhances HIV treatment outcomes. Integration of mental health care into existing health systems has been shown to be effective and cost-efficient in expanding access to mental health services for people with HIV in resource-limited settings. However, more research is needed to identify effective models for integrating HIV and mental health services in various settings. A survey of national HIV program managers revealed that only 38% reported mental health screening in some HIV care settings, with referrals for treatment when indicated. However, 43% lacked mental health screening and treatment services for people with HIV, and no country reported nationwide implementation of such services. The main challenges to integrating mental health services into HIV care include shortages of human resources, limited provider skills and capacity, and insufficient funding. WHO estimates that up to 85% of people with severe mental disorders and 56% of those with depression in lowand middle-income countries lack access to treatment. Screening for depression may support ART adherence, retention in care, and viral load suppression, ultimately improving quality of life. However, implementation requires task-shifting, capacity building for healthcare workers, and adaptation of screening tools for use by non-specialized primary care providers. People living with HIV who use drugs face a range of drug-related disorders, including dependence, intoxication, withdrawal, and overdose. Injecting drug use is associated with various infections and diseases, such as viral hepatitis, tuberculosis (TB), septicemia, and bacterial endocarditis, in addition to HIV. WHO, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), and UNAIDS recommend a comprehensive package of nine interventions for HIV prevention, treatment, and care for people who inject drugs. These include needle and syringe programs, opioid substitution therapy (OST), HIV testing and counseling, ART, prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), condom programs, targeted behavior change communication, prevention and treatment of viral hepatitis, and prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of TB. Nutritional care is critical for people living with HIV, as low energy intake combined with increased energy demands due to HIV infection and related illnesses can lead to weight loss and wasting. Altered metabolism, reduced appetite, and higher rates of diarrhea further contribute to nutrient loss and malnutrition, particularly in low-income and food-insecure settings. Nutritional assessment, counseling, and support should be integral to HIV care, conducted at enrollment and monitored throughout the care continuum. Malnourished patients, especially in food-insecure contexts, may require food supplements alongside ART to support nutritional recovery. Weight loss or failure to maintain a healthy weight at any stage of HIV infection should prompt further assessment and appropriate interventions. For children living with HIV, nutritional assessment is essential to identify malnutrition and growth faltering early. Infants and children should undergo initial nutritional evaluation and regular growth monitoring at each visit, with reference to WHO or national growth curves. Poor growth should trigger further assessment to determine the cause and plan an appropriate response. Nutritional interventions for children living with HIV are detailed in the 2009 guidelines for integrated nutritional care. Palliative care is essential for managing pain and discomfort experienced by people living with HIV at all stages of the disease and during treatment. Providers should address underlying causes where possible while managing pain and ART side effects to support adherence. WHO is currently developing guidelines for palliative care to improve symptom management and end-of-life care for people with HIV. Countries should establish a comprehensive package of general HIV care interventions, in addition to ART, to reduce HIV transmission, prevent illness, and improve quality of life. General care includes basic HIV prevention, health promotion, and screening, prophylaxis, and management of HIV-related coinfections and comorbidities. WHO recommends a package of 13 prevention interventions for adults and adolescents living with HIV in resource-limited settings, including psychosocial counseling, partner notification, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, TB screening and preventive therapy, prevention of fungal infections, STI treatment, reproductive health support, malaria prevention, vaccination, adequate nutrition, family planning, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions.
